title: Take Away, Count Up
child_idea: To find how many are left, take away. To find how far apart two numbers are, count up the gap from the smaller number to the bigger one.

topics: Subtraction within 100 (tens and ones, no renaming)
Subtraction as a gap: how many more, how many fewer
Relation between addition and subtraction (check by adding)
moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only. It is not a claim that the program covers the school syllabus, and it must not appear on child or parent pages as MOE-aligned. Counting up as a subtraction method and the word difference sit inside the Primary 1 subtraction and inverse-relationship outcomes (docs/moe/syllabus_by_level.md, p. 31). The written renaming (borrowing) layout is not taught here.

contest_moves: difference as a gap (how many more)
the gap stays the same when both numbers move by the same amount
objectives: Take away tens and then ones from a number within 100 (no renaming), and say what is left.
Check a subtraction by adding the answer back (57 - 24 = 33 because 33 + 24 = 57).
Find how many more one number is than another by counting up: to the next ten, by tens, then to the number.
Choose a method: count up when the two numbers are close together, take away when the number taken away is small or a whole number of tens.

remember: Bars and squares: a bar is a ten and a square is a one (tens and ones of a number)
Fingers to make 10: how many more to reach the next ten
Count on in tens from any number (34, 44, 54)
joining_cold.assumes: Only counting to 20 and showing a number with fingers. The warm-up teaches the bars and squares again, so a child who missed Lessons 1, 5 and 6 can still join. Taking away small numbers within 10 is done with fingers or objects.
holiday_topics_revisited: Skip counting in 10s (Count with the Frog)
joining_cold.note: Lesson 7 is one of the hardest to miss in Term 1 (plan, section 2). A child who misses it watches the recording and does workbook pages 1 and 2 before Lesson 8. The warm-up carries every idea the lesson needs.

child: The printed workbook (pages 1 to 5) and the kit page (tens bars and ones squares), already cut out by a grown-up
A pencil, a rubber and spare paper
A pencil of a different colour for checking your own work
An envelope or small cup to keep the bars and squares in
tutor: A slide deck and a visible clock or timer slide
Your own set of tens bars and ones squares to show on camera if you wish
kit_pages: Tens bars (9) and ones squares (20), printed on page 6 of the workbook; cut out before the lesson
materials.notes: No ruler is needed. Nothing needs to be bought: the kit page is cut from the workbook. A grown-up does the cutting before the lesson; children never use scissors in the session. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Small things never go near the mouth or ears.

timing.notes: The opening is 2 minutes (the routine and the four inquirer rules were introduced in Lesson 1), so Explore has 16 minutes. The last 5 minutes are the standing buffer; the optional Go further slide is used only if the lesson is on time.

sneak_peek.q1: There are 15 stars. Cross out 4 of them with your pencil. How many stars are left?
sneak_peek.q2: Ali has 58 cards. Ben has 62 cards. How many more cards does Ben have? Write the number, and how you found it.
sneak_peek.a2: 4 more. From 58 to 60 is 2, and from 60 to 62 is 2 more. 2 and 2 make 4.

opening.say: If you are watching the recording: hello! Get a pencil, paper, your workbook and your bars and squares. Pause or rewind any time.
opening.action: Gather your workbook, pencil, paper, and your bars and squares. Press play when ready.

remember.say: Recording: join in! Say the numbers out loud and show your fingers. Pause if you need longer.
remember.action: Play along. Say and show each answer before the video does.

sneak.say: Recording: pause now and try both puzzles on your paper. Guessing is fine. Press play for the next part.
sneak.action: Pause. Try both puzzles on your own paper. A guess is fine.

explore.say: Recording: pause now. Build each number with your bars and squares, then take away or add on. Press play when you have tried.
explore.action: Pause. Build, take away and add on with your bars and squares. Write what you find.

mini.say: Recording: keep watching and copy the examples. Rewind if you miss a step.
mini.action: Watch and copy the examples. Rewind any step you missed.

break.say: Recording: stand up and join in! Small hops to the next ten, big jumps for the tens.
break.action: Stand up. Hop the ones and jump the tens.

work.say: Recording: pause now and do workbook page 1. When you finish a page, press play to check it.
work.action: Pause. Do page 1, then play to check. Then page 2. Then choose a page to try.

talk.say: Recording: pause. Tell a grown-up your answer to the talk question, and say why.
talk.action: Pause. Explain your answer to someone at home, with a reason.

exit.say: Recording: pause and do the exit ticket on your own. Then press play to check it.
exit.action: Pause. Do the exit ticket alone, then play to check it.

look.say: Recording: pause and fill in your look-back box. You can pass.
look.action: Pause. Fill in the look-back box, or pass.

flex.say: Recording: well done for finishing! Show a grown-up one thing you found out.
flex.action: Show a grown-up your workbook and tell them one thing you found out.

lines.text: @rec
Good morning, inquirers! Cameras on, pencil ready, bars and squares on the table. This lesson is recorded for friends who are away. We record me and the screen only. Your camera may be off.
Two towers of blocks stand side by side. One is taller.
Tell your screen or your grown-up: how could we find how much taller?
Today we learn two tools for that: taking away, and counting up.
Greet each child by first name and check their camera shows the page and hands.

Routine and the four inquirer rules were introduced in Lesson 1; do not repeat them. Say the recording notice in your own words: the platform records the tutor and the shared screen only, and a child may keep the camera off.
@rec
A bar is a ten. A square is a one. Look at the picture.
How many bars, how many squares, and what number is it?
Four tens and six ones. We say forty-six. A few more, using fingers or whispers.
Two tens and seven ones. What number?
Five tens and no ones?
Eight tens and three ones?
Fingers to ten. I say a number. Show me how many more fingers make ten.
Seven. How many more to make ten?
Four?
Nine?
Two?
Now count on in tens, starting at thirty-four. Clap on every number.
Count on in tens together: 34, 44, 54, 64, 74. Then say the next ten after a few other starting numbers, such as 6 and 29.
Next, how far to the next ten? It is the same trick as the fingers.
From thirty-eight, how many more to reach forty?
From forty-seven to fifty?
From fifty-six to sixty?

If a child hesitates on 38 to 40 or 47 to 50, show the squares on the slide or your own kit: 38 is 3 bars and 8 squares, and 2 more squares fill the row. Do not move on until most children have answered; counting up to the next ten is the heart of the lesson.

Answers: 46, 27, 50, 83, then 3, 6, 1, 8, then 2, 3, 4. Children answer with fingers, hands or a whispered number. Nobody writes. Joining cold: all you need is counting to 20; the bars and squares are explained on the first slide.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. There are 15 stars. Cross out 4 of them with your pencil. How many stars are left?
Children cross out 4 stars and write how many are left on their own paper.
Puzzle two. Ali has 58 cards. Ben has 62 cards. How many more cards does Ben have? Write the number, and how you found it.
Children write or draw their answer.
Everyone holds their paper to the camera at the same moment, once, after puzzle two. Do not read answers aloud. No private chat.
Thank you. We will come back to puzzle two a little later.

Puzzle 1 answer: 11 stars. Puzzle 2 answer: 4 more (count up 58 to 60 to 62, or 62 take away 58). Look for good ideas to praise later: a child who counted on, who drew two piles, or who used the next ten. Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Today your bars and squares are the teachers. A bar is a ten and a square is a one. First we take away. Build the number I say.
Build fifty-seven: 5 bars and 7 squares.
Children build 57 with their kit.
Take away 2 bars. Put them to one side.
Children move 2 bars away.
What number is left on the table?
Now take away 4 squares.
Children move 4 squares away.
What number is left now?
We took away 2 tens and then 4 ones. That is 24 altogether. Fifty-seven take away twenty-four leaves thirty-three. Tens first, then ones.
Your turn. Build seventy-six. Take away 2 bars and 5 squares. Write what is left on your paper.
Children build 76, take away 2 bars and 5 squares, and write the number left.
What is left? How did you take away?
New question. Ali has forty-seven stickers. Mei has fifty-two stickers. Build Ali's number. Then add pieces until you reach Mei's number.
Children build 47, then add squares until they reach 52.
How many pieces did you add? Tell me how you did it.
We added 3 squares to make a full row of fifty. Then 2 more squares to reach fifty-two. The gap from forty-seven to fifty-two is 5.
One more. Build thirty-eight. Add pieces until you reach sixty-two. Count what you add.
Children build 38 and add squares and bars until they reach 62, counting what they add.
What did you add? How many pieces is that altogether?
Two squares to reach forty. Two bars to reach sixty. Two squares to reach sixty-two. That is 2, and 20, and 2: twenty-four.
What did you notice? When did we take away, and when did we count up?
Taking away tells us what is left. Counting up tells us how big the gap is between two numbers.
A child who counts the pieces left instead of the pieces added: say, this time we are starting at the smaller number and adding on. Count the pieces you put down.
A child with too few squares: ten squares can be swapped for a bar, so there are always enough on the kit page.

Main room only: no breakout rooms, so you can see every camera. Pairs are optional: a grown-up may check the building. Take away: tens first, then ones. Gap: next ten, then tens, then ones. Answers: 37, 33, 51, 5, 24.
@rec
Look. Fifty-seven is 5 tens and 7 ones. Take away 24. First the tens: fifty-seven take away twenty is thirty-seven. Then the ones: thirty-seven take away 4 is thirty-three.
When we took away tens, which digit changed, the tens or the ones?
Subtraction has a friend: addition. If thirty-three and twenty-four make fifty-seven, then we can check. Add the answer back.
If 33 + 24 makes 57, what is 57 take away 33?
Now a different question. Ali has 47 and Mei has 52. How many more does Mei have? The difference is the gap between the two numbers. Count up from 47: 3 to reach fifty, then 2 more.
What is the gap between 47 and 52?
A bigger gap: from 38 to 62. Hop to the next ten. Jump by tens. Hop to the number. Two, then twenty, then two.
How far is it from 38 to 62?
Your turn. Count up to find 81 take away 78. Take away to find 65 take away 23. Write both answers on your paper.
Children write two answers.
Three, and forty-two. 78 to 80 is 2, and 80 to 81 is 1. 65 take away 20 is 45, and 45 take away 3 is 42.
Two tools. Count up when the two numbers are close together. Take away when you take away a small number or whole tens. Both tools give the same answer.
Which tool for 62 take away 59, and which for 62 take away 20?
If a child counts down by ones for 81 - 78, that works too: say, nice, and now let us see if counting up from 78 is shorter.

Key words every time: take away (what is left), count up (the gap), difference (the gap between two numbers). Do not teach the written borrowing layout. Do not teach exchanging a ten for ten ones: the Think harder page uses counting up instead.
@rec
Stand up and get a sip of water. We hop to the next ten, then jump the tens. I say two numbers. You hop and jump the gap.
Call 8 to 30, 25 to 40, 47 to 52, 36 to 71. Children hop the ones to the next ten, jump the tens, hop the last ones. Count the hops and jumps aloud together.
@rec
Page 1, Start here. Question 1: here is 68. Cross out 2 bars and fill in what is left. Question 2: take away. Question 3: take away the tens first, then the ones.
Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor walks the cameras, asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Four tens and eight ones; forty-eight. Thirty-seven, fifty-three, fifty-six, eighty-one. Forty-eight, then forty-three. Mark your own page in another colour.
After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Everyone may choose, at any time.

Page 2. Question 4: take away, then check by adding. Question 5: Mei has 45 stickers and gives 13 away. Draw it. Question 6: Siti says 59 take away 20 is 57. Question 7: a bus has 64 seats and 21 have a child on them.
Page 2, questions 4 to 7.
Thirty-four and forty-six. Thirty-two. No: thirty-nine. Forty-three seats are empty.
When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time.
Choice time: Think harder (page 3), Go further (page 4), the Investigation (page 5), or finish and check your own work. Tutor never says who is on which page.

Q1: ask how many bars are left after you cross out 2. Q5: draw bars as tall rectangles and squares as small boxes. Q6: build 59 with the kit, take away 2 bars, and say what is left. Q7: ask, what does empty mean? Which tool will you use?
Think harder T1 to T4: ask, what is the next ten after the smaller number? How far is that? Then how many tens? Then the last hop. T3: draw two towers, one taller than the other, and add 10 to both.

A child who is still stuck ticks I am still stuck on the look-back page. You check in during the open session in the next lesson (a quick visit to the shared room or a hand signal, parent nearby). Never a private message.
Think harder is for count-up in a new setting. Go further asks which tool is quicker, and why. Do not announce who is on which page. Pairs are never split unless both children agree.
@rec
Ravi finds 52 take away 49 by taking away 40, then 9. Siti counts up from 49. They both get the same answer. Whose way is quicker? Why?
Think for a moment. Use your bars and squares or your fingers if you like.
Talk to the grown-up next to you or to your screen for one minute. Use the sentence starter: I think... because...
Who would like to share? Volunteers first. A pass is always fine.
Remember puzzle two? Ali has 58 cards and Ben has 62. The gap is 4: from fifty-eight to sixty is 2, and 2 more is sixty-two.
Did anyone change their mind about puzzle two while we worked? You can just nod.

Model answer: both answers are 3. Siti is quicker: 49 to 50 is 1, and 50 to 52 is 2. Ravi has to take away 40 and then 9 from 12, which is harder. When two numbers are close, counting up is short. Volunteers first; never call a child by name to answer; no tallies, no rankings. Praise the reason, not the speed.
@rec
Exit ticket. Three questions, on your own, without looking back. Write your answers on page 5.
Children answer E1 to E3 on their own.
Everyone holds their ticket to the camera at the same moment so only you see it. No private chat.
Thirty-four. Five, and five. Three: counting up is quicker because 87 and 90 are close.
Check your own ticket in a different colour. Well done. I will stamp your inquiry journal.

Mark S, D or H in the tutor tracker (tutor only): S = secure on all three, D = developing (one wrong), H = needs help (two or three wrong). If D or H, plan two minutes of catch-up at the start of Lesson 8, in the open session, no names. Do not read out any child's result.
@rec
Look-back. Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. If you like, tick one thing to try next time. You can pass. Nobody reads it out.
Children fill in the look-back box on page 5.
Well done, inquirers. Next lesson is Balance and Swap. You need only a pencil and paper. Goodbye, and thank you to the grown-ups.
Optional, only if you are on time: the gap from 58 to 62 is 4. What is the gap from 59 to 63? And from 68 to 72? What do you notice?
Short think time, then take two answers.
Spare-time menu. If the whole class is ahead, pick one or two activities from the guide (about 4 minutes each).

This is the standing buffer. If you are behind, finish the look-back and say goodbye. Do not start anything new. Optional slide answer: 4 and 4; when both numbers move up by the same amount, the gap stays the same. If the whole class is ahead, use the Spare-time menu (guide section 3b) instead of rushing on.

slides.title: Take Away, Count Up
slides.subtitle: Subtraction: how many are left, and how far apart

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Take away tens and ones, and count up to find a gap.

slides.note: Lesson 7 of Term 1, 90 minutes. Objective: take away tens and ones within 100, count up to find the gap between two numbers, and choose the quicker tool. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8, sneak-peek 8 to 12, explore 12 to 28, mini-lesson 28 to 38, brain break 38 to 42, workbook 42 to 70, talk 70 to 76, exit ticket 76 to 82, look-back 82 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Nobody is told which page they should be on. Tell the group the lesson is recorded (you and the screen only) and that a child may keep the camera off.

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: bars and squares

blocks.text: A bar is a ten. A square is a one.

blocks.label: How many bars? How many squares?

slides.note: Say: a bar is a ten, a square is a one. Children say the number for 4 bars and 6 squares, then the quick-fire three. Answers: 46, 27, 50, 83. This re-teaches tens and ones so a child who has not met them can join. No writing, no marks.

slides.title: Fingers to ten

blocks.text: I show 7. How many more fingers make 10?

slides.note: Say each number; children show on their fingers how many more make ten. Answers: 7 needs 3, 4 needs 6, 9 needs 1, 2 needs 8. Hands up on camera is fine. No writing, no marks. This is the number-bond idea you will use to hop to the next ten.

slides.title: Count on to the next ten

blocks.text: Start at 34. Count on in tens. Clap each one.
How many more from 38 to reach 40?

slides.note: Count on in tens from 34 (34, 44, 54, 64, 74) with a clap on each number. Then ask the next-ten questions: 38 to 40 is 2, 47 to 50 is 3, 56 to 60 is 4. Use the squares and a full row if a child is unsure. This is the hop you will use all lesson.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: There are 15 stars. Cross out 4 of them.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: How many more cards does Ben have?
Write the number, and how you found it.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (15 stars, cross out 4) is an access question: any child can try it by crossing out and counting. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson idea, the gap between two numbers. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Everyone holds the paper to the camera once, at the same moment, after puzzle 2; there is no private chat and no board in front of the group. Answers: 11; 4 more. Do not reveal Puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores.

slides.title: Explore: take away

items: Take away 2 bars. What is left?
Take away 4 squares. What is left?

blocks.head: YOUR TURN
items: Build 76. Take away 2 bars and 5 squares.

slides.note: Round 1, about 6 minutes. Objects first, no writing yet except the final number. Children build 57, take away 2 bars (37), then 4 squares (33). Then they build 76 and take away 2 bars and 5 squares (51). Ask how they took away. Key idea: tens first, then ones. A child with few squares can swap ten squares for a bar; the kit page has enough.

slides.title: Explore: how far to go?

blocks.text: Build the smaller number. Add pieces until you reach the bigger number.

slides.note: Round 2, about 7 minutes, main room. Ali has 47 and Mei has 52: children add 3 squares to make 50, then 2 more to make 52, so the gap is 5. Then 38 to 62: 2 squares to make 40, 2 bars to make 60, 2 squares to make 62: 2 + 20 + 2 = 24. Children count what they add, not what they have. Ask them to say it as hop, jump, hop.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: What does the gap tell us?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key idea: taking away tells us what is left; counting up tells us how far apart two numbers are, the difference. Repeat a child's answer in your own words so the recording picks it up. Both tools use the same bars and squares.

slides.title: Take away tens, then ones
slides.note: Think aloud: 57 is 5 tens and 7 ones. Take away 2 tens first: 37. Then take away 4 ones: 33. The picture on the right is what is left. Ask: which digit changes when we take away tens? Answer: the tens digit. Keep it to about a minute; children have just done this with the kit.

slides.title: Check by adding
slides.note: Show that the answer plus the number taken away gives back the start. 33 + 24 = 57, so 57 - 24 = 33 is right, and also 57 - 33 = 24. Ask: if 33 + 24 makes 57, what is 57 take away 33? Answer: 24. This is the relation between addition and subtraction, with no new vocabulary.

slides.title: How many more? The gap
slides.note: The difference between two numbers is the gap. Start at the smaller number and count up to the bigger: 47 to 50 is 3, 50 to 52 is 2, so the gap is 5. Ask: what is the gap between 47 and 52? Answer: 5. Say it as how many more: Mei has 5 more than Ali.

slides.title: Count up in jumps

blocks.text: Hop to the next ten. Jump by tens. Hop to the number.

slides.note: Think aloud: from 38 hop 2 to reach 40; jump 2 tens to reach 60 (that is 20); hop 2 to reach 62. Add the hops and the jump: 2 + 20 + 2 = 24. Ask: how far is it from 38 to 62? Answer: 24. This is the same count as the explore with the bars and squares.

slides.title: Your turn

blocks.text: Write on your paper. Timer: 1 minute

slides.note: Each child writes on their own paper. Walk the cameras. Do not ask children to hold boards up in front of the group. The first is a short gap, so counting up is quick; the second is a small number of tens and ones, so taking away is quick.

slides.title: Check: your turn
slides.note: Answers: 3 and 42. Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group.

slides.title: Choose your tool

rows: the two numbers are close together
you take away a small number or whole tens

blocks.text: Both tools give the same answer.

slides.note: Ask: which tool for 62 take away 59, and which for 62 take away 20? Answer: count up for the first (3), take away for the second (42). This is the rule of thumb the Go further page asks children to explain. Both tools give the same answer; choosing is about being quick and being right.

slides.title: Hop to the ten, jump the tens

blocks.text: Small hops to the next ten. Big jumps for the tens.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera. Call each pair of numbers and have children hop the ones to the next ten, jump the tens, then hop the last ones; count the hops and jumps aloud. Gaps: 22, 15, 5, 35. No equipment. Keep it gentle for small spaces.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here
slides.note: Read questions 1 and 2 aloud. Children work on their own; the tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. After question 3 any child may choose to carry on or try Think harder.

slides.title: Check page 1
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children mark their own page in a different colour. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group.

slides.title: Workbook page 2: Start here
slides.note: Read question 6 aloud: it is a spot-the-mistake. Read question 7 aloud as well. Children may draw bars and squares to decide. Question 4 asks them to check by adding.

slides.title: Check page 2
slides.note: Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Question 6 answer: no, 39, because she took away 2 ones instead of 2 tens. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group.

slides.title: Choose your next page

rows: Count up in a new setting
Finish and check your own work

blocks.text: Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time.

slides.note: Invite the whole group at once, for example: when you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Never announce who is on which page and never name a child. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Model answers are in the tutor guide. About 4 minutes.

slides.title: Talk and explain

blocks.head: RAVI AND SITI
items: Ravi finds 52 - 49 by taking away 40, then 9.

slides.note: One minute of talk to the grown-up next to you, or to your screen. Then volunteers first; a pass is always fine; never call a child by name to answer. Model answer: both get 3. Siti is quicker, because 49 and 52 are close: 49 to 50 is 1, and 50 to 52 is 2. Repeat each child's answer in your own words for the recording.

slides.title: Back to the sneak-peek

blocks.text: Ben has 4 more cards than Ali.

slides.note: Reveal puzzle 2 now. Say: many of you wrote a good reason. Do not read out anyone's earlier answer. The gap from 58 to 62 is 2 and 2, which is 4. Some children will have taken away 62 - 58 or counted on one by one: all are good.

slides.title: Exit ticket

blocks.text: On your own. No looking back. Timer: 3 minutes

slides.note: Children answer on page 5. After the timer everyone holds the ticket to the camera at the same moment, so only the tutor sees it (no private chat). Stamp the inquiry journal.

slides.title: Check the exit ticket
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children check their own ticket in a different colour.

slides.title: Look-back
slides.note: Three minutes. Children tick or write the look-back box on page 5. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out. If a child ticks I am still stuck, check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared room or a hand signal, parent nearby); never a direct message. At the start of the next lesson you may say to the whole group: today you could try drawing it, using objects or checking your answer.

mascot.say: Take your time. You can pass.

slides.title: Well done, inquirers!

blocks.text: Show a grown-up one thing you found out today.

blocks.head: NEXT LESSON
items: You need a pencil and paper.

slides.note: Say goodbye and thank the grown-ups. Minutes 85 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If you ran late, finish any open item (stamps, the look-back). Do not start anything new. If the whole class is ahead, show the optional menu slide and use the Spare-time menu from the tutor guide.

slides.title: Go further: what if?

blocks.text: What is the gap from 59 to 63? And from 68 to 72?

slides.note: Optional, only if you are on time. Answer: 4 and 4. Both numbers move up by the same amount, so the gap stays the same. Take two answers and move on. This is the same idea as Think harder question 3.

slides.title: If we have time: pick one

rows: Add 10 to both numbers. Does the gap stay the same?
Write a gap story for your grown-up
Show how to count up from 58 to 62

slides.note: Optional Spare-time menu, used only if the whole class is ahead. Pick one or two activities (3 to 5 minutes each); full tutor lines and answers are in the tutor guide. Never start new content and never name who is ahead. Slow down with how do you know rather than rushing on. These minutes come from the flex buffer and are not part of the 90-minute sum.

start.text: Here is 68 as bars and squares. Cross out 2 bars. Fill in what is left.
start.hint: A bar is a ten. Cross out 2 bars, then count the bars and squares that are left.
start.solution: 68 is 6 tens and 8 ones. Take away 2 tens: 4 tens and 8 ones are left. That is 48. The ones did not change.
mistakes: Crossing out 2 squares instead of 2 bars (66).

start.text: Take away. Use your kit if you like.
start.hint: Taking away tens changes the tens digit. Taking away ones changes the ones digit.
start.solution: (a) 5 tens take away 2 tens is 3 tens: 37. (b) 7 ones take away 4 ones is 3 ones: 53. (c) 8 tens take away 3 tens is 5 tens: 56. (d) 6 ones take away 5 is 1: 81.

start.text: Take away the tens first, then the ones. Find 68 - 25.
start.hint: 25 is 2 tens and 5 ones. Take away the 2 tens first. Then take away the 5 ones from what is left.
start.solution: 68 take away 20 is 48. Then 48 take away 5 is 43. So 68 - 25 = 43.

start.text: Take away. Then check by adding the answer back.
start.answer: 34, then 46 (the same as the start, so it checks)
start.hint: Take away 1 ten, then 2 ones. To check, add 12 to your answer. Do you get 46 back?
start.solution: 46 take away 10 is 36, and 36 take away 2 is 34. Check: 34 + 12 = 46, the number we started with. So 46 - 12 = 34 is right.
mistakes: Not adding back the number taken away (adding 46 + 12).

start.text: Mei has 45 stickers. She gives 13 away. Draw 45 as bars and squares. Cross out 13. How many are left?
start.answer: 32 (4 bars and 5 squares drawn; 1 bar and 3 squares crossed out)
start.hint: Draw 4 bars and 5 squares. Cross out 1 bar and 3 squares. Count what is left.
start.solution: 45 is 4 tens and 5 ones. 13 is 1 ten and 3 ones. 45 take away 10 is 35. 35 take away 3 is 32. So Mei has 32 left.

start.text: Siti says 59 - 20 = 57. Is she right? Write the right answer, and say what she did.
start.answer: No. 39. She took away 2 ones instead of 2 tens (57 is 59 - 2).
start.hint: Build 59 with your kit. Take away 2 bars, not 2 squares. What is left?
start.solution: 59 is 5 tens and 9 ones. Take away 2 tens: 3 tens and 9 ones, which is 39. Siti took away 2 ones, so she got 57.

start.text: A bus has 64 seats. 21 seats have a child on them. How many seats are empty?
start.hint: Empty seats are the seats left when we take away the seats with a child. Take away the 2 tens first.
start.solution: 64 take away 20 is 44. Then 44 take away 1 is 43. So 43 seats are empty.

think.text: Mei has 62 beads. Ravi has 38 beads. How many more beads does Mei have? Count up from 38: to the next ten, then by tens, then to 62.
think.hint: 38 needs 2 more to reach 40. Then jump by tens to 60. Then hop to 62. Add up the hops and the jump.
think.solution: 38 to 40 is 2. 40 to 60 is 20. 60 to 62 is 2. The whole gap is 2 + 20 + 2 = 24. Check: 38 + 24 = 62.

think.hint: What is the next ten after 77? How far is it? Then how far from that ten to 83?
think.solution: 77 to 80 is 3. 80 to 83 is 3. The gap is 3 + 3 = 6. Check: 77 + 6 = 83.

think.text: Ali has 24 stickers. Ben has 31 stickers. Each child gets 10 more stickers. Now how many more stickers does Ben have than Ali?
think.answer: 7 more (the gap stays the same: 34 and 41, and 41 - 34 = 7)
think.hint: Work out how many stickers each child has now. Or draw two towers and add the same 10 to both.
think.solution: Ali now has 34 and Ben has 41. The gap from 34 to 41 is 7. It was 7 before too (24 to 31), because both children got the same 10 more.

think.text: A book has 71 pages. Ravi has read 46 pages. How many pages are left to read? Count up from 46.
think.answer: 25 pages (46 to 50 is 4, 50 to 70 is 20, 70 to 71 is 1)
think.hint: Start at 46. Hop to the next ten, jump by tens, then hop to 71. Add up all the hops and jumps.

go.text: Ravi wants to find 71 - 68 and 71 - 20. Which tool is quicker for each, take away or count up? Write why. Then find both answers.
go.answer: 71 - 68 = 3 (count up: the numbers are close). 71 - 20 = 51 (take away: 2 tens).
go.hint: For 71 - 68, how far is it from 68 up to 71? For 71 - 20, what happens to the tens digit?
go.solution: 71 - 68: count up. 68 to 70 is 2 and 70 to 71 is 1, so 3. The numbers are close, so the gap is short. 71 - 20: take away 2 tens to get 5 tens and 1 one, which is 51. Counting up 20 would be a long way.
mistakes: Taking away 68 from 71 one at a time.

go.text: A crate holds 100 eggs. 64 eggs are sold. How many eggs are left? Find it two ways, take away and count up. Do the two answers match?
go.answer: 36 eggs. Take away: 100 - 60 = 40, then 40 - 4 = 36. Count up: 64 to 70 is 6, then 70 to 100 is 30, so 36. They match.
go.hint: Take away: take away the 6 tens, then the 4 ones. Count up: hop from 64 to 70, then jump by tens to 100.
go.solution: Take away: 100 - 60 = 40, and 40 - 4 = 36. Count up: 64 to 70 is 6, and 70 to 100 is 30, so 6 + 30 = 36. Both ways give 36. Check: 64 + 36 = 100.
mistakes: Writing 40 (forgetting to take away the 4 ones).

go.text: Mei says 83 - 47 and 86 - 50 have the same answer. Is she right? Find both answers and say why.
go.answer: Yes. Both are 36. Both numbers go up by 3, so the gap does not change.
go.hint: Count up from 47 to 83 for the first. Take away 5 tens for the second. Then look at how 83 and 47 changed.
go.solution: 83 - 47: 47 to 50 is 3, 50 to 80 is 30, 80 to 83 is 3, so 36. 86 - 50 = 36. 83 became 86 and 47 became 50: both went up by 3, so the gap between them stayed 36.
mistakes: Saying the answers differ because the numbers differ.

investigation.title: When is counting up quicker?
investigation.first: Find 52 - 49 and 52 - 10. Try take away and count up for each. Which way was quicker each time?
investigation.text: Make up three subtractions where counting up is quicker, and three where taking away is quicker. What do you notice about the two numbers?
investigation.answer: Counting up is quicker when the two numbers are close together, so the gap is short (52 - 49 is 3). Taking away is quicker when the number taken away is small or a whole number of tens (52 - 10 is 42). If the numbers are far apart and the small number is awkward, both ways take longer.
val: small or whole tens: take away
investigation.look_for: A child who tries several pairs, says what they notice about how far apart the numbers are, and gives a reason. Accept any clear rule that matches examples. A child who also checks by adding is doing well.
mistakes: Choosing a tool without looking at how far apart the numbers are.
Saying one tool is always quicker (it depends on the numbers).

talk.question: Ravi finds 52 - 49 by taking away 40, then 9. Siti counts up from 49. They both get the same answer. Whose way is quicker? Why?
talk.answer: Siti's way is quicker. 49 to 50 is 1, and 50 to 52 is 2, so the answer is 3. The numbers are close together, so the gap is short. Ravi's way gets 3 too, but he has to take away 9 from 12.
talk.look_for: A reason about the numbers being close, with the hops (1 and 2). Praise any clear reason; both ways are right.

exit.solution: 58 take away 20 is 38, and 38 take away 4 is 34.
57 to 60 is 3, and 60 to 62 is 2. That is 5. So 62 - 57 = 5.

exit.text: To find 90 - 87, which is quicker: take away or count up? Write the answer.
exit.answer: 3. Counting up is quicker: 87 and 90 are close together.
exit.solution: 87 to 90 is 3, so 90 - 87 = 3. Counting up is quick because the numbers are close.
mistakes: Taking away 87 from 90 one at a time.

home_practice.text: A jar has 78 sweets. 20 are eaten. How many sweets are left?
home_practice.solution: 78 is 7 tens and 8 ones. Take away 2 tens: 5 tens and 8 ones, which is 58.

home_practice.text: Take away, then check by adding: 76 - 43 = ___ . Check: ___ + 43 = 76.
home_practice.solution: 76 take away 40 is 36, and 36 take away 3 is 33. Check: 33 + 43 = 76.

home_practice.text: Take away the tens first, then the ones: 89 - 36 = ___
home_practice.solution: 89 take away 30 is 59. 59 take away 6 is 53.

home_practice.text: Ben has 47 cards. Ali has 71 cards. Who has more, and how many more? Count up.
home_practice.answer: Ali has 24 more (47 to 50 is 3, 50 to 70 is 20, 70 to 71 is 1)

home_practice.text: At home: open a book at two page numbers, such as 38 and 71. Find how many pages from one to the other two ways: by taking away and by counting up. Do the two ways match?
home_practice.answer: Any two pages: for example 38 and 71: 71 - 38 = 33, and counting up 38 to 40 is 2, 40 to 70 is 30, 70 to 71 is 1, so 33. Both ways match.
home_practice.solution: A grown-up checks that the child adds the hops and jumps, then adds the answer back to the smaller page number to get the bigger one.

online_practice.title: Take Away, Count Up
online_practice.topic: Subtraction within 100: take away and count up

items.hint: Take away 2 tens. The ones stay the same.
steps: Take away 2 tens: 3 tens and 8 ones.

slips.say: 56 takes away 2 ones. Take away 2 tens (20) instead.
78 is 58 + 20. We take away.

tpl.hint: Take away {t} tens. The ones stay the same.
steps: {a} is made of tens and ones.

items.hint: Take away 3 ones. The tens stay the same.

46 takes away 3 tens. Take away 3 ones instead.

steps: {a} is made of tens and ones.
Take away {o} ones. The tens do not change.

items.q: What is 68 - 25? Take away the tens, then the ones.
items.hint: 25 is 2 tens and 5 ones. Take away 2 tens first, then 5 ones.

slips.say: 93 is 68 + 25. We take away.
53 is 68 - 15. Take away 2 tens, not 1.

tpl.q: What is {a} - {b}? Take away the tens, then the ones.
tpl.hint: {b} is {tb} tens and {ob} ones. Take away the tens first, then the ones.

items.q: A bus has 86 seats. 32 seats have a child on them. How many seats are empty?
items.hint: Empty seats are what is left when we take away the seats with a child.

slips.say: 118 is 86 + 32. Empty means we take away.

tpl.q: A bus has {a} seats. {b} seats have a child on them. How many seats are empty?
tpl.hint: Empty seats are what is left when we take away the seats with a child.
steps: Take away the tens of {b} from {a}.

items.hint: To check a take away, add the answer back to the number you took away. Do you get the start?
steps: The answer is 33. The number taken away is 24.
57 is the number we started with, so the take away is right.

items.q: Ben has 38 stickers. Mei has 62 stickers. How many more stickers does Mei have than Ben?
items.hint: Count up from 38: hop to the next ten, jump by tens, hop to 62.

slips.say: 100 is 38 + 62. We want the gap between them.
36 does not count the 2 tens jump. 40 to 60 is 20.

tpl.q: Ben has {x} stickers. Mei has {y} stickers. How many more stickers does Mei have than Ben?
tpl.hint: Count up from {x}: hop to the next ten, jump by tens, hop to {y}.
steps: Start at {x}. Count up to the next ten.
Jump by tens, then hop to {y}.
Add the hops and jumps: the gap is {ans}.

items.hint: What is the next ten after 58? How far is it? Then how far to 62?

slips.say: 120 is 62 + 58. We want the gap.
14 takes away 48. Count up from 58 to 62.

tpl.hint: What is the next ten after {b}? How far is it? Then how far to {a}?
steps: Hop from {b} to the next ten.

items.q: Ali has 24 stickers. Ben has 31 stickers. Each child gets 10 more stickers. Now how many more stickers does Ben have than Ali?
items.hint: Find each child's new number. Or think: both got the same 10 more.
steps: Ali now has 34. Ben now has 41.
The gap was 7 before, because both got the same amount.

slips.say: 17 is 7 + 10. Both children get 10, so the gap does not change.
41 is Ben's number now. We want how many MORE than Ali.

tpl.q: Ali has {a} stickers. Ben has {b} stickers. Each child gets {c} more stickers. Now how many more stickers does Ben have than Ali?
tpl.hint: Find each child's new number. Or think: both got the same {c} more.
steps: Find the gap between the two new numbers.

items.q: To find 82 - 79, which way is quickest?
options: Take away 7 tens, then take away 9 ones
items.hint: Look at the two numbers. Are they close together or far apart?
steps: Counting up gives 3 in two short steps, so it is quickest.

slips.say: Adding gives a bigger number. We want the gap between them.

items.q: A crate holds 100 eggs. 64 eggs are sold. How many eggs are left?
items.hint: Count up from 64: hop to the next ten, then jump by tens to 100.

slips.say: 164 is 100 + 64. Eggs were sold, so take away.
46 is 100 - 54. Count up from 64.

tpl.q: A crate holds 100 eggs. {n} eggs are sold. How many eggs are left?
tpl.hint: Count up from {n}: hop to the next ten, then jump by tens to 100.
steps: Hop from {n} to the next ten.
Add the hop and the jumps: {ans} eggs are left.

items.q: 83 - 47 = 86 - ___. What number goes in the blank?
items.hint: 83 went up by 3 to make 86. What must 47 do so the gap stays the same?
steps: The top number went up by 3: 83 to 86.
The bottom number must go up by 3 too: 47 to 50.

slips.say: 47 is the number we started with. The top number went up, so the bottom number goes up too.
44 is 47 - 3. Add the same number to both.

tpl.q: {a} - {b} = {a2} - ___. What number goes in the blank?
tpl.hint: {a} went up by {c} to make {a2}. What must {b} do so the gap stays the same?
steps: The top number went up by {c}.
The bottom number must go up by {c} too.

items.q: Ali has fewer stickers than Mei. The gap is 24. Mei has 71. How many stickers does Ali have?
items.hint: Ali is 24 below Mei. Take away the gap from Mei's number.

slips.say: 95 is 71 + 24. Ali has fewer, so take away.
24 is the gap. Ali has the number 24 below Mei.

tpl.q: Ali has fewer stickers than Mei. The gap is {g}. Mei has {m}. How many stickers does Ali have?
tpl.hint: Ali is {g} below Mei. Take away the gap from Mei's number.

items.q: Make up a story about the gap between two numbers, like two piles or two towers. Find the gap by counting up. Then check by adding.
items.hint: Pick two numbers first, one bigger than the other. Then write the story.
steps: Write the two numbers in your story and ask how many more.
Count up from the smaller number: hop to the next ten, jump by tens, hop to the bigger number.

Check: the smaller number plus your gap should make the bigger number. For example: Ali has 47 cards and Ben has 71 cards. 47 to 50 is 3, 50 to 70 is 20, 70 to 71 is 1, so the gap is 24. Check: 47 + 24 = 71.

parent.summary: We learned two ways to find the answer to a subtraction. To find how many are left, we take away the tens, then the ones. To find how far apart two numbers are (the difference), we count up the gap: hop to the next ten, jump by tens, hop to the number. Your child built numbers with bars and squares, took them away, and counted up gaps such as 38 to 62.
words: take away: find what is left (57 - 24 = 33)
count up: find the gap from the smaller number to the bigger one
difference: the gap between two numbers
check: add the answer back to the number taken away
try_home: Two piles: make two piles of small things, such as 38 and 62 coins or buttons. Ask: how many more in the big pile? Count up the gap together: hop to the next ten, jump by tens, hop to the number.
Take it away: say a number up to 80 and a number of tens and ones to take away, such as 68 take away 25. Take the tens first, then the ones. Then check by adding the answer back.
Spot it: look at two page numbers, two house numbers or two ages. Ask: how far from one to the other? Which way is quicker, taking away or counting up?
ask: Which is quicker here, taking away or counting up? Why?
How can you check your answer?
parent.when_stuck: Please let your child use real things or draw bars and squares, and wait 10 seconds before helping. Asking what is the next ten? works better than giving the answer.
parent.next: Lesson 8: Balance and Swap. Your child needs a pencil and paper only.
parent.report_line: Your child is learning to see numbers as tens and ones, to notice patterns and to say why. This week: taking away tens and ones, and counting up to find the gap between two numbers.
parent.term_line: Your child is learning to see numbers as tens and ones, to notice patterns and to say why.
parent.quote: The difference is a gap. Take away to see what is left. Count up to see the gap.

workbook.hint_p1: Use your kit, a drawing or your fingers. Say your answer out loud, then write it.
workbook.hint_p3: Use your kit, draw a picture or count up. Then write how you know. Choose any question, in any order.

kits.title: Kit page: tens bars and ones squares
kits.intro: A grown-up cuts these out before the lesson. A bar is a ten. A square is a one. Keep them in an envelope.

safeguarding: The kit pieces stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. A grown-up cuts out the kit page before the lesson; children do not use scissors in the session.
This lesson uses the main room only: no breakout rooms, so the tutor sees every camera. A parent sits nearby but does not give answers.
Sneak-peek and exit answers are shown on the child's own paper to the camera at the same moment, once. There is no private chat and no board held up in front of the group.
Never read out a child's name with a right or wrong answer. Never show a child's page in the recording; record the tutor and the screen only, with children's video excluded.
A child who ticks I am still stuck gets a check-in in the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared room or a hand signal, parent nearby). No private messages to children.
The look-back is never collected in front of the group or read out. A pass is always allowed.
tutor_prep: Solve every workbook question yourself first, both by taking away and by counting up.
Tell parents a week before: print workbook pages 1 to 6, cut out the kit page (page 6) and keep the bars and squares in an envelope.
Have your own bars and squares ready to show on camera, and have the slides open with the timer slide visible on screen share.
Check the recording settings exclude children's video.

spare_time.note: Optional time, never added to the 90-minute sum. It comes from the 5-minute flex buffer, from slack in the parts, or from the optional Go further slide.
rules: Whole class ahead: use the Spare-time menu in the Flex time and the optional Go further slide. Pick one or two activities; do not start new content.
A few children ahead: they may choose Go further or the Investigation, which are open to everyone. Never label or name a child, and never announce who is ahead.
Never teach anything the next lesson needs. If the class is ahead, slow down: ask "How do you know?" and let children explain, rather than rushing on.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: if you add 10 to both numbers, the gap stays the same. Try 12 and 20, then 22 and 30, then 32 and 40. Is Mei always right?
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Try the gap from 12 to 20, then 22 to 30. Is the gap the same?
menu.answer: Yes. 12 to 20 is 8, 22 to 30 is 8, 32 to 40 is 8. Both numbers move up by the same amount, so the gap stays the same.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Write a short story about the gap between two numbers, such as two plants of different heights or two piles of cards. Give it to your grown-up to solve by counting up.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Write a gap story with two numbers for a grown-up to solve.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check that the story has two numbers and asks how many more, and that counting up and adding back agree.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never counted up. Teach them how to find the gap from 58 to 62.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Teach a grown-up how to count up from 58 to 62.
menu.answer: 58 to 60 is 2, and 60 to 62 is 2, so the gap is 4. Hop to the next ten, then hop to the number.
